summary.text: 听 is the standardized simplified form of 聽, meaning “hear” or “listen.” It also has a separately attested older use meaning “smiling appearance”; the evidence does not connect the two meanings by semantic development.

formation.text: For the older word meaning “smiling appearance,” the received analysis treats 听 as phonosemantic: 口 supplies a mouth-related meaning category, and 斤 is assigned the sound role. This account does not explain how 听 came to represent 聽.

components.text: In the received analysis of the older smiling-word use, 口 contributes a mouth-related meaning category. This role is scoped to that historical use of 听.
The received account assigns 斤 the sound role in the older smiling-word graph. Reported historical readings are available, but the evidence does not establish a matched component–host comparison.

sound_limitation.text: The reported Zhengzhang forms for 听 and 斤 are not matched by the evidence, so they do not establish a same-system component–host sound comparison. The supplied Baxter–Sagart readings do not cover the older smiling word and 斤 as a pair; modern Mandarin readings do not establish their ancient sound relationship.

sound.text: A Zhengzhang transcription reports *kɯn and *kɯns for 斤, but the cited evidence does not match either form to a particular reading of the older 听 word.
Modern Mandarin readings are 斤 jīn and 听 tīng. This current pair does not establish a historical sound relation for the older smiling-word sense.

history.text: The curated glyph is a modern redraw in Shuowen seal-script style, associated with 听’s older “smiling appearance” use. It is not an excavated artifact and does not establish a sequence of graphic changes.

A secondary proposal traces the graph’s right side through an intermediate 𠯸 containing 厅, later copied so that 厅 was assimilated to 斤. This proposed pathway has not been verified from primary manuscript evidence.
听 is the standardized simplified counterpart of 聽 and was used for 聽 in Song–Yuan vernacular writing. This graphic relationship does not show that the older smiling-word use developed from 聽.

uncertainties.text: Han- and Tang-period literary examples attest the smiling sense, but do not establish its first occurrence. The date and textual path by which 听 came to represent 聽 are unresolved.

The proposed 𠯸-to-听 pathway and its 厅 sound component lack independent confirmation from primary manuscript evidence. Historical readings for 听 and 斤 are reported, but the evidence does not establish a matched comparison.

senses.period: Han-period example cited; exact first attestation unresolved
senses.text: A Han-period literary example uses 听 for a smiling appearance. This attestation does not establish when the word or graph first arose.

senses.period: Song–Yuan vernacular use attested; beginning date unresolved
senses.text: By the Song–Yuan period, 听 was used to write the separate word 聽, meaning “hear” or “listen.” Why this graph was reused is unresolved; the proposed 𠯸/厅 account has not been verified from primary manuscript evidence.

limitations.text: The smiling and hearing/listening uses are separately documented. No semantic development from “smiling appearance” to “hear” or “listen” is supported.

items.caption: This seal-script-style form is associated with the older 听 word meaning “smiling appearance.” The received Shuowen analysis assigns 口 a semantic role and 斤 a phonetic role; the pictured right side is curved, and the redraw alone does not establish that analysis.
items.alt: Black seal-script-style glyph with two upright strokes joined by a crossbar on the left and a broad curved form on the right.
items.selection_reason: It illustrates the form associated with the older smiling-word account, while keeping the received component interpretation separate from what the image visibly shows.
